Lied
līd
v. (past tense of lie: to speak falsehood with intent to deceive; rendering Hebrew kazab and kachash, Greek pseudomai)
Old English leogan, to lie. The Hebrew kazab means to fail or be found false, as a brook that dries in summer; the Greek pseudomai gives English pseudo-.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version records the sin in ascending seriousness. An old prophet in Bethel stops a man of God on the road and claims an angelic revision of his orders — “But he lied unto him” (1Ki 13:18) — and the younger man, who had withstood a king, is destroyed by a lie from a fellow prophet. Asaph records the nation's religion: “they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues” (Psa 78:36), lying to God in the very act of worship. Isaiah presses the cause: “of whom hast thou been afraid or feared, that thou hast lied, and hast not remembered me?” (Isa 57:11) — the fear of man is the engine of falsehood, and forgetting God is what makes it possible. Then Ananias in the church, and Peter's word: “thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God” (Act 5:4). That sentence is the doctrine of the whole subject. Every lie is told in the hearing of God, and it is finally told to Him. Lying is not merely socially corrosive; it is a direct assault on the character of the God who cannot lie, and Revelation twice puts liars outside the city with sorcerers and murderers.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to lie as to utter falsehood with an intention to deceive, or with an immoral design; and lied as the past tense, having uttered such falsehood.

LIE, v.i. To utter falsehood with an intention to deceive, or with an immoral design.

Thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.

LIED, pret. of lie. Uttered falsehood with intent to deceive.

Key Scripture

1Ki 13:18 — "He said unto him, I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the LORD, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him."

Psa 78:36 — "Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues."

Isa 57:11 — "And of whom hast thou been afraid or feared, that thou hast lied, and hast not remembered me, nor laid it to thy heart? have not I held my peace even of old, and thou fearest me not?"

Modern Corruption

The lie has been reclassified as a social lubricant — the harmless untruth, the necessary exaggeration, the curated self — and the biblical account of it as an assault on God's own nature has been quietly filed away.

expand to see more

Peter's sentence to Ananias is the doctrine in nine words: thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God. Ananias had told a manageable lie about a manageable sum in a voluntary offering, and by any ordinary reckoning it was a small deceit inside a generous act. Scripture reckons otherwise, because the audience of every lie is God. Modern moral vocabulary has almost no room left for this. Untruth is graded by its social consequences — the white lie, the harmless exaggeration, the professionally necessary spin, the presented self that everyone knows is edited — and where consequences are small, guilt is assumed to be small. But Titus 1:2 grounds our hope in a God that cannot lie, and Revelation 21:8 and 22:15 place liars outside the city in company that startles every reader. The reason the sin is treated so gravely is that it is a direct contradiction of the divine character in the creature made to image it. Isaiah 57:11 supplies the usual cause and it is worth self-examination: of whom hast thou been afraid? Almost every lie a Christian tells can be traced to a fear of some man, and the cure is the fear of God, which drives out the other.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kazab (H3576), to lie, to fail as a deceitful brook; kachash (H3584), to deceive, deny, or dissemble; Greek pseudomai (G5574), to speak falsely.

expand to see more

Hebrew kazab (H3576) — to lie, to prove false; the noun is used of a brook whose waters fail in the heat; 1 Kings 13:18, Jeremiah 15:18.

Hebrew kachash (H3584) — to deceive, to deny, to feign submission; Isaiah's charge against the idolatrous nation; Isaiah 57:11, Joshua 7:11.

Greek pseudomai (G5574) — to speak falsely, to lie; Peter's word to Ananias, and Paul's command that the new man lie not one to another; Acts 5:4, Colossians 3:9.

Usage

"“But he lied unto him” — a prophet destroyed by a prophet's falsehood."

"“They lied unto him with their tongues” — lying to God in the act of worship."

"“Thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God” — the audience of every lie."
